title: The Power And Pitfalls Of Letting Students Learn Through Experience
author: Natalie Wexler
summary: Natalie Wexler starts from a vivid memory of a sixth-grade medieval England simulation to ask when experiential learning is worth using. Drawing on Greg Ashman's book on explicit teaching, she explains why direct instruction works better: working memory is easily overloaded by projects, and students remember whatever they spend the most time thinking about, which is often castle-building rather than the Middle Ages. She then catalogues simulations that went seriously wrong, including slave auctions and Nazi role-play, and notes that a study of social studies simulations found 12 of 14 had significant problems. She allows that simulations and well-designed projects can work when students first have knowledge built through explicit instruction, when sensitive topics are handled carefully and teachers are well trained. Her conclusion is that, absent excellent training and support, teachers should lean primarily on direct instruction, supplemented by narratives and writing.
points: Projects and simulations add to cognitive load and direct attention to procedure rather than content.
Wexler distinguishes the strong emotional reactions simulations provoke from the understanding they are meant to build, with real harm in several documented cases.
Simulations are safest after explicit instruction has given students the knowledge, and when students are not pitted against one another.
Research on simulations in social studies classes found most had pointless, aimless or inaccurate designs, reflecting teachers' lack of training.
First-person narratives, historical novels and strong writing assignments can deliver the empathy aim with less risk.
quotes: Having a clear explanation or “worked example” can ease the cognitive burden. And engaging in projects or simulations can add to it in ways that impede learning.

Also, students are most likely to remember whatever they spend the most time thinking about. If they’re learning about the Middle Ages by making a detailed model of a castle, they’ll probably remember more about the process of constructing the castle—figuring out what materials to use, making them fit together—than anything about the Middle Ages.

That’s not to say that kids should just get lectures. Teachers also need to check frequently to make sure students understand the material. They need to ask questions or assign activities that require practice and analysis. But the basic idea is that the teacher should be directing rather than merely facilitating learning.

That mindset is surely one reason teachers are drawn to activities that are largely student-directed and active. But they probably also sense that—as Ashman’s title says about explicit teaching—experiential learning can be powerful. In fact, sometimes it’s too powerful.

There are ways to make simulations work, but they require careful thought and planning. Before students undertake a simulation, they need to have adequate knowledge of the topic—ideally built through explicit instruction.
One study of simulations in social studies classes—titled “Try Not to Giggle if You Can Help It”—found that 12 of 14 had significant problems.
I remember concepts like villeinage and strip-farming from my sixth-grade study of Medieval England, but it’s not because I wiped my hands on the dog. I’m sure my teacher explained them to me.
